title: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere
answer: When this Volume began, the raw material was a stack of 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists. Reading them one by one felt like walking through a crowded market where every stall sold something slightly different.

papers.why: Its famous subtitle question, where are the educators, is the same gap the newer K12 studies still report. The four category taxonomy is a useful secondary lens for Chapter 2 alongside the book's ten patterns.
papers.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
papers.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education (Springer)
papers.caveat: Higher education, pre 2019, pre generative AI.
papers.finding: Systematic review of 146 of 2,656 articles (2007 to 2018) on AI in higher education. Four application areas with 17 subcategories: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalization, and intelligent tutoring systems. Field dominated by computer science and STEM authors and quantitative methods. Almost no critical reflection on risks, weak connection to pedagogical theory, few longitudinal or implementation studies.

papers.why: The most cited framing paper in the field and a strong support for the book's grade band approach, the fact checking habit, and the equity chapters.
papers.title: ChatGPT for good? On opportunities and challenges of large language models for education
papers.venue: Learning and Individual Differences (Elsevier)
papers.caveat: Position paper, early 2023, no empirical classroom data.
papers.finding: Position paper from a large multidisciplinary German team. Large language models can generate educational content, improve engagement, and personalize learning across ages from children to adults. Using them well requires teachers and learners to build competencies to understand the technology and its brittleness, plus a clear system strategy and a pedagogy centered on critical thinking and fact checking. Recommends protocols for fact checking model output, regular review of models for curriculum uses, transparent information on what models can and cannot do, and age appropriate interfaces (gamified and less machine like for children, critical thinking and fact checking focus for older learners). Flags unequal access for non English speakers and for under funded schools.

papers.why: Frames the vendor dependence and data control risk that the book treats in Chapter 3 and the board chapter: districts buy tools whose design choices shape teaching.
papers.title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
papers.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning (Springer)
papers.caveat: Conceptual, higher education, 2017, before generative AI. No empirical data.
papers.finding: Early conceptual paper on AI in higher education. Argues AI will take over many tasks at the core of teaching practice, that tools already in use (learning management systems, plagiarism detectors) raise the question of who sets the teaching agenda, corporations or institutions, and that concentration of AI in a few tech companies creates privacy and control risks. Calls on institutions to rethink teacher roles and pedagogy now.

papers.why: Provides the vocabulary for Chapter 3's approved tool review and the argument that ethics covers pedagogy (what the tool makes students do), not only data privacy.
papers.title: Ethics of AI in Education: Towards a Community-Wide Framework
papers.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer)
papers.caveat: Small response rate; researcher opinion, not school practice.
papers.finding: Survey of leading AI in education researchers (17 of 60 invited responded) on ethics. Good intentions are not enough: the field must address fairness, accountability, transparency, bias, autonomy, agency, and inclusion, and distinguish doing ethical things from doing things ethically, including the ethics of pedagogical choices and unintended consequences. Most researchers are not trained to handle the emerging ethical questions. Argues for a multidisciplinary ethics framework with practical guidelines, ethical by design.

papers.why: The standard K12 AI literacy frame cited across our library and the natural spine for the book's grade band AI literacy progression in Chapter 20 and the appendix.
papers.title: Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI?
papers.venue: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
papers.caveat: Short 2019 position paper, pre generative AI; later AI4K12 materials expand it and should be checked for the current version, which is not verified here.
papers.finding: Launch paper for the AAAI and CSTA AI4K12 national guidelines. Defines Five Big Ideas every K12 student should learn: computers perceive the world through sensors; agents maintain models of the world and reason with them; computers can learn from data; intelligent agents need many kinds of knowledge to interact naturally with humans; AI can affect society positively and negatively. Gives grade band expectations, for example K to 2 identify how AI appears in daily life, 3 to 5 think critically about impacts such as self driving cars and jobs, 6 to 8 compare AI to earlier industrial revolutions, 9 to 12 evaluate new AI technologies and their ethical questions and build simple chatbots and sentiment tools. The initiative sets guidelines and curates resources rather than writing a curriculum.

papers.why: Supports context-specific, participatory PD for teachers rather than generic AI courses.
papers.title: Empowering educators to be AI-ready
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence (Elsevier)
papers.caveat: Framework paper; example from higher ed.
papers.finding: Luckin et al. define AI Readiness: contextualised, participatory training that helps each profession understand data-driven AI in its own setting, not generic AI learning. Presents a step framework and a higher education example at Arizona State University. Also describes AIED systems for learners, teachers (dashboards relaying tutor insights), and institutions.

papers.why: The strongest evidence in the library for the book's hints not answers theme and for the claim that tool design, not tool presence, decides whether AI helps or harms. It also shows students cannot judge the harm themselves, which supports configured tools over open access for younger grades.
papers.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
papers.venue: PNAS
papers.caveat: One school, one subject, short term outcomes only, run in Fall 2023 with GPT-4; math has objective answers that writing lacks. The guardrailed tutor prevented harm but did not produce a learning gain.
papers.finding: Randomized field experiment with nearly 1,000 students at one Turkish high school, Fall 2023, math review sessions. Three arms: a plain ChatGPT style GPT-4 chat (GPT Base), a guardrailed GPT-4 tutor (GPT Tutor), and no AI. With access during practice, grades rose 48 percent (Base) and 127 percent (Tutor). On a later exam without AI, the Base group scored 17 percent worse than students who never had AI; the Tutor group's harm was essentially eliminated but showed no gain. Base users mostly asked for and copied solutions (a crutch); Tutor users asked for help and attempted answers. Students did not perceive that copying hurt their learning. Guardrails: the prompt included each problem's solution (to curb hallucination), an instruction not to give away the full solution, and teacher supplied common mistakes with matching hints.

papers.why: The clearest positive counterpart to the PNAS harm study: the same class of model improved learning when paired with tutor style prompts, teacher supervision, and curriculum alignment. The authors credit the whole package, not the chatbot alone, which is the book's central argument about implementation over technology.
papers.title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
papers.venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125
papers.caveat: License recorded from OpenAlex as CC BY; the PDF text extracted here does not state its license, so this is not verified from the document itself. Six weeks, nine urban Benin City schools with computer labs, after school, volunteers, English only. Effect estimates partly reflect extra instructional time with a teacher present; no teacher only tutoring arm.
papers.finding: Randomized trial in nine senior secondary schools in Benin City, Nigeria, June to July 2024. First year senior secondary students (about age 15) attended up to twelve 90 minute after school lab sessions over six weeks, working in pairs with Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) on English topics aligned to the national curriculum. Each session opened with a teacher provided prompt designed to make the model act as a tutor, not an answer giver, using learning science principles such as retrieval practice; teachers circulated and kept students on task, and sessions closed with group reflection. Teachers received three days of training. Result: 0.31 standard deviation gain on a combined assessment (0.23 on English), equal to roughly 1.5 to 2 years of typical schooling, placing it among the most cost effective education programs. Largest gains for girls and higher achieving students. Worked despite internet and power outages.

papers.why: Best evidence in the library that AI aimed at the adult, not the child, improves learning, and that it helps the least experienced adults most. Directly supports the book's Chapter 20 argument that AI should raise teacher and tutor quality, and gives a cost figure a board member can compare against a $3,300 per teacher PD program the authors cite.
papers.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
papers.venue: arXiv (cs.CL), Stanford
papers.caveat: Preprint, chat based tutoring platform, one district, two months, novice tutors. Proximal outcomes improved; end of year tests did not. Effects depend on tutors actually using the tool.
papers.finding: First randomized controlled trial of a human and AI system in live K12 tutoring: 900 novice tutors and 1,800 students from historically under served communities (majority Hispanic) in a Southern US school district, two months, math, preregistered. Tutor CoPilot gives the human tutor real time, expert like suggestions, not the student. Students of tutors with access were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics (62 to 66 percent exit ticket pass rate); students of lower rated tutors gained 9 points; students of tutors who actually used it gained 14 points. Cost was about $20 per tutor per year. Across 550,000 messages, tutors with access asked more guiding questions and gave away fewer answers. Tutors flagged suggestions that were not grade level appropriate or were too advanced. No significant effect on end of year state math scores.

papers.why: Best single citation for the state of K-12 AI evidence.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in K-12 education: An umbrella review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Review of reviews; inherits input quality.
papers.finding: Umbrella review of 102 systematic reviews of AI in K-12. AI supports instruction, personalization, engagement and collaboration, automated assessment and feedback, and content management. Challenges: technical limits, pedagogical hurdles, ethical risks, systemic barriers. Calls for more reviews on AI education and literacy.

papers.why: Human-like avatars can import bias into AI tutoring.
papers.title: Face value: How avatar identity shapes epistemic trust in AI-mediated learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Two experiments (N=102, N=294): AI tutor avatar race, gender, and age shaped credibility and whether learners used the guidance. White avatars, and Asian male avatars in STEM, were rated more credible; older Black female avatars were penalized. STEM tasks amplified bias.

papers.why: Design notes for girls-in-computing AI programs.
papers.title: Beyond “painting in pink”: A critical case study of all-girls generative AI workshops in a European makerspace and implications for gender equity in computing
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: All-girls GenAI makerspace workshops: representation, relationship building, and responsive teaching supported girls; challenges included poor topic choice and limited peer interaction.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: Large language models in education: a systematic review of empirical applications, benefits, and challenges
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of empirical LLM applications in education, benefits and challenges.

papers.why: School climate shapes later AI dependence; autonomy support matters in high school.
papers.title: How high-school pressure and autonomy support are linked to dual AI learning pathways: A cross-contextual SEM analysis
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: 508 university students recalling high school: high-school pressure linked to controlled motivation, then compulsive AI use and lower wellbeing; autonomy support linked to constructive use.

papers.why: Background on thinking outcomes.
papers.title: The cognitive impact of ChatGPT in higher education: A systematic review of critical and creative thinking outcomes
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Systematic review of ChatGPT effects on critical and creative thinking in higher education.

papers.why: Background; not K-12.
papers.title: Undergraduate students’ learning outcomes with ChatGPT: A meta-analytic study
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of undergraduate learning outcomes with ChatGPT.

papers.why: AI in class does not close SES gaps; teach digital skills explicitly.
papers.title: Decoding divides: The role of socioeconomic status and personality traits in AI divides and educational inequality
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: 4,497 Dutch Grade 6 students: digital literacy, not amount of AI use, mediated links between personality traits and achievement. Family SES advantage was direct and not changed by classroom AI use.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: Learning with machines: Toward a theory of epistemic co-agency
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Theory of epistemic co-agency in learning with machines.

papers.why: Students with disabilities are rarely studied; text-only design excludes some.
papers.title:
Exploring Artificial Intelligence Integration and Student‐
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Interaction in K‐12 Education: A Scoping Review
papers.venue: Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
papers.finding: Scoping review of 70 K-12 student-AI studies (2014-2023): few reported student diversity; chatbots and tutors dominate; input is mostly single-modality text.

papers.why: Warning about offloading; supports hints-not-answers and metacognition.
papers.title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking
papers.venue: Societies
papers.finding: 666 participants: frequent AI use correlated with lower critical thinking, mediated by cognitive offloading; younger people more dependent.

papers.why: Large pooled effects exist but likely inflated by short, small studies; motivation boost fades.
papers.title: Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on K-12 and Higher Education Students’ Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
papers.venue: Journal of Educational Computing Research
papers.caveat: Mixed study quality; mostly higher ed.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 49 studies: GenAI mean effect 0.86 on achievement and 0.80 on motivation, larger in higher education; novelty effect on motivation fades over time.

papers.why: Current map of K-12 GenAI uses with named risks.
papers.title: A Systematic Review of Generative AI in K–12: Mapping Goals, Activities, Roles, and Outcomes via the 3P Model
papers.venue: Systems
papers.finding: Review of 84 K-12 GenAI studies (ages 3-18). Seven objectives and five activity patterns; roles shift from AI-directed to AI-supported. Risks: hallucinations, less originality, over-reliance, motivational loss, ethics.

papers.why: Shows elementary evidence is thin.
papers.title: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review
papers.venue: Frontiers in Education
papers.finding: Review of 30 K-12 GenAI studies: mostly high school and pre-service teachers, STEM focus, quasi-experimental, psychological outcomes.

papers.why: Connects GenAI to Universal Design for Learning.
papers.title: Harnessing the Power of Generative AI to Support ALL Learners
papers.venue: TechTrends
papers.finding: Summer 2023 teacher institute: most teachers had never used GenAI; 43% believed it would make instruction more accessible for all learners; UDL strategies for English learners and students with disabilities.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: AI & learning: A preferred future
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Author leads the vendor behind the India reading platform (id 97).
papers.finding: Opinion piece on a preferred future for AI in learning: autonomous learners, learning science, multisensory engagement.

papers.why: Supports human decides, AI assists framing.
papers.title: Human and artificial cognition
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Argues AI is already shaping information we see; near-term focus should be human-AI collaboration in sensemaking and decisions.

papers.why: Clean frame to explain why hints-not-answers and student agency matter; maps to Bastani's guardrail finding.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in education: The three paradigms
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Position paper: three paradigms, AI-directed with learner as recipient, AI-supported with learner as collaborator, AI-empowered with learner as leader. Trend is toward learner agency.

papers.why: Supports the book's claim that long-term evidence is thin.
papers.title: AI technologies for education: Recent research & future directions
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Review of 40 empirical AIEd studies (1993-2020). Summarizes applications and benefits and calls for attention to ethics and privacy and for large, longitudinal, interdisciplinary research.

papers.why: Early source for the book's pilot-small-measure-scale theme and for teacher co-design. Its warning that tools stall at prototype still describes many school purchases.
papers.title: Intelligence Unleashed: An argument for AI in Education
papers.venue: Pearson Open Ideas report (UCL Knowledge Lab)
papers.caveat: 2016, pre-generative AI; published by a commercial education company; argument, not evidence.
papers.finding: Pearson/UCL argument for AI in education. Explains learner, pedagogical, and domain models; AI teaching assistants and learning companions. Warns AIEd research mostly tackles structured domains, rarely leaves prototype stage, and lacks classroom evidence. Recommends: start with learning not technology; involve teachers, students, parents in co-design; evaluate in real settings; shared data standards that prioritize ethics; smart demand from buyers for tools proven to work.

children.name: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
children.blurb: Draft, then a person edits is the simplest and most common pattern in this volume.

children.name: Pattern 2: The Human Review Gate
children.blurb: The Human Review Gate is a limit on AI, not a use of it: certain decisions must be made by a person, with AI only informing.

children.name: Pattern 3: Adaptive Practice
children.blurb: Adaptive practice is software that watches how a student answers and changes the next question, giving harder items after a run of correct answers and easier ones after a run of mistakes.

children.name: Pattern 4: Hints, Not Answers
children.blurb: Hints, Not Answers is the fourth of the book's ten patterns, and it means an AI tutor is set up to ask questions and offer clues instead of handing over the solution.

children.name: Pattern 5: Early Warning, Then a Person Reaches Out
children.blurb: Pattern 5 is an early warning approach that combines attendance, grades, behavior records, and screening results to flag a student who may be slipping, then sends a person to reach out.

children.name: Pattern 6: Language Access
children.blurb: Language Access is the sixth pattern in the book's set of ten patterns that show up everywhere.

children.name: Pattern 7: Speech as a Bridge
children.blurb: Speech as a Bridge is the seventh of the book's ten patterns, and it uses speech technology to give students a way around a barrier rather than a way past the learning itself.

children.name: Pattern 8: Feedback Before Grades
children.blurb: Feedback Before Grades is a pattern where AI gives students comments on a draft before a teacher grades the final version.

children.name: Pattern 9: Scheduling and Logistics
children.blurb: Pattern 9 is the use of optimization software for behind the scenes school logistics such as bus routes, master schedules, substitute placement, lunch forecasts, and heating and cooling.

children.name: Pattern 10: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale
children.blurb: Pattern 10 says a school should test an AI tool with a small group of teachers for a set time, measure one meaningful result, and then decide to expand, adjust, or stop.

children.name: For Parents: Thinking For or Helping to Think
children.blurb: This idea gives parents a plain way to tell whether AI at school is doing their child's thinking or helping the child think.

sections.body: This section is about ten patterns that show up across school life from preschool to graduation. The book began with 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists, and found that nearly every idea and all 300 ideas in the Volume fit one of ten patterns. A pattern is a way of dividing the work between a machine and a person, saying what the AI does, what the adult does, and where the adult checks the result. The chapter takes the patterns one at a time, with examples from early grades, middle grades, and high school where the pattern reaches that far, and it gives the first pattern the longest treatment because it accounts for more ideas than any other. It closes with a short test any parent can use to tell whether AI at school is doing the thinking or helping a child do it.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that the patterns matter because tools change fast, and of 125 products checked while the Volume was researched, 81 could not be confirmed on age rules, privacy terms, or prices and were left out, while others changed terms during drafting. What works is asking which pattern a tool follows and who the person is in that pattern, then keeping an updated tool inventory with a pattern and an owner named for every tool. A vendor's description or a list of features is not evidence, and what counts is a plain statement of how the school actually uses the tool and who checks its work. The common failure is a tool that fits no pattern cleanly, drafting, grading, and flagging all at once, so nobody is sure which part a person should check, and over time the checking quietly stops because no one was named to do it. The rule the book holds to is that a pattern must name what the AI does, what the adult does, and where the adult checks the result, and research held for this chapter fits that rule, as in Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, where a guardrailed tutor reduced harm, and Tutor CoPilot, where human tutors with real time suggestions asked more guiding questions and gave away fewer answers.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits is the first stop for a teacher or leader who wants to see the pattern that accounts for more ideas than any other, and it shows where a person must edit what the AI drafts. Pattern 2: The Human Review Gate and Pattern 3: Adaptive Practice show how a person checks AI work and how practice adjusts, while Pattern 4: Hints, Not Answers and Pattern 5: Early Warning, Then a Person Reaches Out show how AI can prompt rather than solve and how a person makes the call after a warning. Pattern 6: Language Access and Pattern 7: Speech as a Bridge are for teachers who need AI to help with language and spoken communication, and Pattern 8: Feedback Before Grades and Pattern 9: Scheduling and Logistics are for feedback that comes before a grade and for the logistics that keep a school running. Pattern 10: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale is for leaders who need to test one pattern carefully before spreading it, following the Thirty Day Move and Figure 2.7, and For Parents: Thinking For or Helping to Think is the short test a parent can use to tell whether AI is doing the thinking or helping a child do it. Together these pages let a teacher, leader, or parent go to the pattern that matches the question they have, rather than judging a tool by its brand or feature list.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
